Archie vs building it yourself.

The parts are all free and public. If you enjoy this sort of thing, you can absolutely build your own agent, and this page will not pretend otherwise.

Archie is in testing. The waitlist hears the day it opens. See where it stands → Checked against the sources below on August 19, 2026.

The short answer

Same idea. The difference is who does the plumbing.

Both paths run on hardware you own, talking to an AI company on your own account, so custody is not a reason to pick us over your own build: you would have it either way. What you are choosing is whether the plumbing is your evenings or ours.

Where Archie wins

Four things you do not have to build, or keep building.

Everything here is finished, and it stays finished when the services behind it change.

The connections are done

Calendar, mail, files, a to-do list and meeting notes, connected on a picker with the tokens in your computer’s password storeSource 6, and kept working when a provider changes what it accepts.

The approval gate is built in, and cannot be switched off

A proposed calendar change and a drafted email wait for you. It is enforced in code, not asked for in a promptSource 5.

Add-ons are data, not code

A skill is instructions, not a program, so there is nothing to compile, nothing to sandbox and nothing to break when Archie updates itself. Every add-on in the store is includedSource 3.

Archie outlives us

Our Terms require a final build that needs no sign-in if we stopSource 2.

Side by side

What you take on, either way.

Archie compared with self-hosting your own agent, across setup, connectors, maintenance, control and cost
  Archie Your own build
Getting to a first working agent Install it and answer a few questions An evening at minimum, longer with real accounts wired in
Connecting your accounts A picker, with the tokens kept in your computer’s password storeSource 6 Yours to write, and yours to store safely
Approval before anything sends Built in, and it cannot be skippedSource 5 Yours to build, and easy to leave until later
Keeping it running Updates arrive. What stays yours is the computer: it has to be on and awake, for either of these Yours: dependencies, breaking API changes, the lot
Changing how it behaves Instructions and add-ons, in the app Anything you like. This is the real prize
If the company behind it disappears Our terms commit us to publishing a final build that needs no sign-inSource 2 Nothing to disappear
What you pay $30Source 4 a month, plus your own AI usage Your own AI usage, and your time

The self-hosted column is written from what the open tools publish about themselves rather than from a benchmark of our own; n8n’s Community edition is the concrete example cited at the foot of this pageSource 1. How long a build takes you depends on you, which is why that row is in words.

Where your own build wins

Four things your own build does better.

All four are real, and they are what your evenings buy you.

You can read every line

Archie is not open source. You can watch what it sends with a network monitor, and our Trust page shows you how, but you cannot read the source. With your own build, you can.

No subscription, and nobody to trust

No plan, no sign-in, no company that could change its mind. That is a real advantage. What we put against it is in writing rather than in good intentions: our Terms require that if Otian ever ceases operations, we publish a final version of Archie that requires no license check, within 30 days.

Your own build can do anything you can write

Our add-ons are instructions and settings rather than codeSource 3, which is a deliberate safety decision and also a ceiling. Your own build has no ceiling.

You can run the model locally too

A build of your own can point at a model running on your own computer and never touch an AI company at all. Archie connects to a hosted provider, so on that one axis a local model beats every hosted setup, ours included.

Worth saying

We built Archie because we got tired of rebuilding it.

The first versions of this were exactly that: hand-built setups, one per person, held together by whoever made them. What you are paying for is that the fiddly parts are finished and stay finished.

Sources for every figure and claim on this page
1A self-hostable example

n8n publishes a self-hostable Community edition on GitHub under its Fair-code licence, listed on n8n.io/pricing, read on August 19, 2026. It is named here as one concrete instance of the free-and-public path, not as the only one.

2The final-build commitment

Our Terms require us to publish a version that needs no sign-in if we cease operating. The wording is in the Terms of Service and the reasoning is on the Trust page.

3Add-ons are data, not code

An add-on is written instructions and settings; Archie has nowhere to run code an add-on brings with it. That is why the ceiling above is real, and it is documented on the Trust page.

4Archie, $30 a month

Our own price, with the AI usage that sits on top of it broken down on the pricing page.

5Approval before anything sends

Email and calendar changes are drafted and held for approval in the app. The mechanism, and the honest limit on it, are on the Trust page.

6Where your account tokens sit

Archie keeps the tokens for your connected accounts in your computer’s own password store. What that means, and every outbound connection it makes, are on the Trust page.

On local models

Said plainly because it is true: a locally run model is more private than a hosted one, and Archie uses hosted providers. Our claim has always been about custody, that no server of ours holds your content, and never about being the most private option available.

Rather not spend the evenings on a build?
